With the last two statements (from the print of ieee_rint(2.5, round) on) removed, the program builds warning-free with gfortran 16.2 and prints the first seven lines above unchanged.

Source: J3/23-007r1: 17.4 The rounding modes, 17.11.8 IEEE_GET_ROUNDING_MODE, 17.11.11 IEEE_INT, 17.11.36 IEEE_RINT and 17.11.42 IEEE_SET_ROUNDING_MODE

Reading the output:

  • In round-to-nearest the sum of ten 0.1 values in real32 is 1.0000001192, one ulp above 1. In to-zero and down it is 0.99999982119, below 1, and up gives 1.0000002384. The same ten additions give three different answers depending on the mode. This is the basis of interval arithmetic: compute the same expression once with ieee_down and once with ieee_up and the true result lies between.

  • 1/3 is 0.3333333433 in nearest and up, and 0.3333333135 in to-zero and down, the two real32 numbers that surround one third.

  • ieee_rint(x) rounds to an integral value in the current mode. With nearest, 2.5 goes to 2 and 1.5 to 2 (ties to even), 0.5 to 0.0 and -0.5 to -0.0, which has the sign of the argument (17.11.36). Up and down give the directed results.

  • ieee_support_rounding is false for ieee_away and ieee_other: the hardware has no such mode.

Rounding mode and formatted output interact. A conversion from binary to decimal in a write also has a rounding mode: the input/output rounding mode of 13.7.2.3.8, set by round= on open or on the data transfer statement, or by the RN, RZ, RU, RD, RC and RP edit descriptors, and by default processor_defined. GNU Fortran takes the processor-defined mode from the current floating-point rounding mode, Flang does not:

program io_rounding
  use, intrinsic :: iso_fortran_env, only: real32
  use, intrinsic :: ieee_arithmetic, only: ieee_set_rounding_mode, ieee_nearest, ieee_to_zero, ieee_support_io
  implicit none
  real(real32) :: third
  third = 1.0_real32/(3.0_real32 + real(command_argument_count(), real32))
  print '(a, l1)', 'ieee_support_io: ', ieee_support_io(third)
  print '(a, es18.10e3)', 'round-to-nearest mode          : ', third
  call ieee_set_rounding_mode(ieee_to_zero)
  print '(a, es18.10e3)', 'round-to-zero mode, default I/O: ', third
  write (*, '(a, rn, es18.10e3)') 'round-to-zero mode, RN edit   : ', third
  call ieee_set_rounding_mode(ieee_nearest)
end program io_rounding

gfortran 16.2:

ieee_support_io: T
round-to-nearest mode          :  3.3333334327E-001
round-to-zero mode, default I/O:  3.3333334326E-001
round-to-zero mode, RN edit   :  3.3333334327E-001

Source: J3/23-007r1: 13.7.2.3 Real and complex editing (13.7.2.3.8 input/output rounding mode), 17.11.42 IEEE_SET_ROUNDING_MODE and 17.11.58 IEEE_SUPPORT_IO

Flang 23 prints 3.3333334327E-001 on all three lines. Source: J3/23-007r1: 13.7.2.3.8 Input/output rounding mode and 17.11.58 IEEE_SUPPORT_IO

The lesson is to restore the mode before printing numbers, as the rounding example does, or to select the I/O rounding explicitly with an edit descriptor.

Underflow mode and subnormals

Some processors let a program choose between gradual underflow (results below tiny become subnormal numbers, the IEEE behaviour) and abrupt underflow (they flush to zero), which can be faster. ieee_support_underflow_control(x) says if the control exists for the kind of x, ieee_get_underflow_mode(gradual) reads it and ieee_set_underflow_mode(gradual) sets it, and the standard forbids calling the two subroutines when the inquiry is false for every kind (restriction of 17.11.10 and 17.11.44). The underflow mode affects only reals of kinds for which the inquiry is true (17.5). The program below uses ieee_get_modes and ieee_set_modes to restore the mode in one call, and refuses to run the procedures when the control is not available.

program underflow_mode
  use, intrinsic :: iso_fortran_env, only: real32, real64
  use, intrinsic :: ieee_arithmetic
  implicit none
  real(real32) :: t32, h32
  real(real64) :: t64, h64
  logical :: gradual
  type(ieee_modes_type) :: saved

  print '(a, 2(1x, l1))', 'support underflow_control (real32, real64): ', ieee_support_underflow_control(1.0_real32), &
    ieee_support_underflow_control(1.0_real64)
  print '(a, 2(1x, l1))', 'support subnormal         (real32, real64): ', ieee_support_subnormal(1.0_real32), &
    ieee_support_subnormal(1.0_real64)

  t32 = tiny(1.0_real32)*real(1 + command_argument_count(), real32)
  t64 = tiny(1.0_real64)*real(1 + command_argument_count(), real64)

  if (.not. ieee_support_underflow_control(1.0_real32) .or. .not. ieee_support_underflow_control(1.0_real64)) then
    ! calling the underflow-mode procedures would violate their restrictions (17.11.10, 17.11.44)
    print '(a)', 'underflow mode cannot be controlled for these kinds on this processor and compiler'
  else
    call ieee_get_modes(saved)
    call ieee_get_underflow_mode(gradual)
    print '(a, l1)', 'initial underflow mode is gradual: ', gradual
    h32 = t32/2.0_real32
    h64 = t64/4.0_real64
    print '(a, es14.6e3, a, l1)', 'gradual : tiny/2 (real32) = ', h32, '  subnormal: ', ieee_class(h32) == ieee_positive_subnormal
    print '(a, es14.6e3, a, l1)', 'gradual : tiny/4 (real64) = ', h64, '  subnormal: ', ieee_class(h64) == ieee_positive_subnormal

    call ieee_set_underflow_mode(.false.)
    call ieee_get_underflow_mode(gradual)
    print '(a, l1)', 'after ieee_set_underflow_mode(.false.), gradual: ', gradual
    h32 = t32/2.0_real32
    h64 = t64/4.0_real64
    print '(a, es14.6e3, a, l1)', 'abrupt  : tiny/2 (real32) = ', h32, '  subnormal: ', ieee_class(h32) == ieee_positive_subnormal
    print '(a, es14.6e3, a, l1)', 'abrupt  : tiny/4 (real64) = ', h64, '  subnormal: ', ieee_class(h64) == ieee_positive_subnormal

    call ieee_set_modes(saved)                ! one call restores rounding, underflow and halting modes
    call ieee_get_underflow_mode(gradual)
    print '(a, l1)', 'after ieee_set_modes(saved), gradual: ', gradual
  end if
end program underflow_mode

On gfortran 16.2 on aarch64 the inquiry is false for both kinds and the program says so:

support underflow_control (real32, real64):  F F
support subnormal         (real32, real64):  T T
underflow mode cannot be controlled for these kinds on this processor and compiler

Flang 23 supports the control for real32 and real64:

support underflow_control (real32, real64):  T T
support subnormal         (real32, real64):  T T
initial underflow mode is gradual: T
gradual : tiny/2 (real32) =  5.877472E-039  subnormal: T
gradual : tiny/4 (real64) =  5.562685E-309  subnormal: T
after ieee_set_underflow_mode(.false.), gradual: F
abrupt  : tiny/2 (real32) =  0.000000E+000  subnormal: F
abrupt  : tiny/4 (real64) =  0.000000E+000  subnormal: F
after ieee_set_modes(saved), gradual: T

Source: J3/23-007r1: 17.5 Underflow mode, 17.7 The floating-point modes and status, 17.11.10 IEEE_GET_UNDERFLOW_MODE, 17.11.44 IEEE_SET_UNDERFLOW_MODE and 17.11.64 IEEE_SUPPORT_UNDERFLOW_CONTROL

In abrupt mode tiny / 2 is zero where gradual underflow gives the subnormal 5.877E-39. Programs that compile with -ffast-math may also have the flush-to-zero bit set at program start (see the compiler options section), without any call to ieee_set_underflow_mode.

The IEEE functions in practice

Neighbours, scaling, remainder, signs and fused multiply-add

ieee_next_after(x, y) returns the representable number next to x in the direction of y (and x if they are equal). The neighbours of zero are nonzero, the neighbour of huge toward infinity is infinity, and the difference ieee_next_after(x, +1) - x equals spacing(x). ieee_logb(x) returns the unbiased exponent as a real, equal to exponent(x) - 1, and ieee_scalb(x, i) is x * 2**i, exact whenever the result is representable. ieee_rem(x, y) is the IEEE remainder: x - y*n with n the integer nearest to x/y, so unlike mod, whose result has the sign of x, it can be negative for positive operands. ieee_copy_sign is defined for every IEEE value, including NaN and infinity. ieee_fma(a, b, c) computes a*b + c with a single rounding, and signals overflow, underflow and inexact according to the final result.

program functions
  use, intrinsic :: iso_fortran_env, only: real32, real64
  use, intrinsic :: ieee_arithmetic
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = real64
  real(dp) :: one, x, nan, pz, nz
  real(real32) :: xs

  one = 1.0_dp + real(command_argument_count(), dp)
  x = 0.1_dp*one
  nan = ieee_value(one, ieee_quiet_nan)
  pz = 0.0_dp*one
  nz = -pz

  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'x                       = ', x
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'next_after(x, 1)        = ', ieee_next_after(x, 1.0_dp)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'next_after(x, 0)        = ', ieee_next_after(x, 0.0_dp)
  print '(a, l1)', 'next_after(x, 1) - x == spacing(x): ', ieee_quiet_eq(ieee_next_after(x, 1.0_dp) - x, spacing(x))
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'next_after(+0, 1)       = ', ieee_next_after(pz, 1.0_dp)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'next_after(+0, -1)      = ', ieee_next_after(pz, -1.0_dp)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'next_after(huge, +Inf)  = ', ieee_next_after(huge(x), ieee_value(x, ieee_positive_inf))
  print *
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'ieee_logb(10)           = ', ieee_logb(10.0_dp*one)
  print '(a, i0, a, i0)', 'exponent(10) = ', exponent(10.0_dp*one), ', so ieee_logb = exponent - 1 = ', exponent(10.0_dp*one) - 1
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'ieee_scalb(3, 4)        = ', ieee_scalb(3.0_dp*one, 4)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'ieee_rem(5, 3)          = ', ieee_rem(5.0_dp*one, 3.0_dp*one)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'mod(5, 3) for contrast  = ', mod(5.0_dp*one, 3.0_dp*one)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'ieee_rem(7, 4)          = ', ieee_rem(7.0_dp*one, 4.0_dp*one)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'ieee_copy_sign(2, -0)   = ', ieee_copy_sign(2.0_dp*one, nz)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'ieee_copy_sign(NaN, -1) = ', ieee_copy_sign(nan, -one)
  print '(a, 2(1x, l1))', 'ieee_signbit(+0), ieee_signbit(-0): ', ieee_signbit(pz), ieee_signbit(nz)
  print *
  ! fused multiply-add: a*b + c with a single rounding
  xs = 1.0_real32 + 2.0_real32**(-12)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'a*a - 1 with two roundings   = ', real(xs*xs - 1.0_real32, dp)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'ieee_fma(a, a, -1), one round = ', real(ieee_fma(xs, xs, -1.0_real32), dp)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'exact value of a*a - 1       = ', real(xs, dp)**2 - 1.0_dp
  print *
  print '(a, l1, 2x, a, l1, 2x, a, l1)', 'ieee_selected_real_kind(15, 300) = kind 8: ', ieee_selected_real_kind(15, 300) == 8, &
    'sp kind 4: ', ieee_selected_real_kind(6, 37) == 4, 'no such kind: ', ieee_selected_real_kind(40) < 0
end program functions

Output (identical with Flang 23):

next_after(x, 1)        =  1.00000000000000019E-001
next_after(x, 0)        =  9.99999999999999917E-002
next_after(x, 1) - x == spacing(x): T
next_after(+0, 1)       =  4.94065645841246544E-324
next_after(+0, -1)      = -4.94065645841246544E-324
next_after(huge, +Inf)  =                  Infinity

ieee_logb(10)           =  3.00000000000000000E+000
exponent(10) = 4, so ieee_logb = exponent - 1 = 3
ieee_scalb(3, 4)        =  4.80000000000000000E+001
ieee_rem(5, 3)          = -1.00000000000000000E+000
mod(5, 3) for contrast  =  2.00000000000000000E+000
ieee_rem(7, 4)          = -1.00000000000000000E+000
ieee_copy_sign(2, -0)   = -2.00000000000000000E+000
ieee_copy_sign(NaN, -1) =                       NaN
ieee_signbit(+0), ieee_signbit(-0):  F T

a*a - 1 with two roundings   =  4.88281250000000000E-004
ieee_fma(a, a, -1), one round =  4.88340854644775391E-004
exact value of a*a - 1       =  4.88340854644775391E-004

ieee_selected_real_kind(15, 300) = kind 8: T  sp kind 4: T  no such kind: T

Source: J3/23-007r1: 17.11.3 IEEE_COPY_SIGN, 17.11.4 IEEE_FMA, 17.11.16 IEEE_LOGB, 17.11.25 IEEE_NEXT_AFTER, 17.11.35 IEEE_REM, 17.11.37 IEEE_SCALB, 17.11.38 IEEE_SELECTED_REAL_KIND and 17.11.51 IEEE_SIGNBIT

Points to notice:

  • next_after(+0, -1) is the negative smallest subnormal, -4.94E-324: the neighbours of zero in both directions are nonzero.

  • ieee_rem(5, 3) is -1 (5/3 is nearest to 2, and 5 - 3*2 = -1) where mod(5, 3) is 2, and ieee_rem(7, 4) is -1; the standard’s own examples are ieee_rem(4, 3) = 1, ieee_rem(3, 2) = -1 and ieee_rem(5, 2) = 1. ieee_rem is exact (no rounding error) and is the right tool for argument reduction.

  • The fused multiply-add computes a*a - 1 for a = 1 + 2^-12 in real32 as the correctly rounded value of the exact result, 4.8834E-04, where the two-step computation first rounds a*a and ends with 4.8828E-04: the low bits of the product are lost.

  • ieee_selected_real_kind(15, 300) is kind 8 and a request that no kind satisfies gives a negative result (17.11.38).

The newer functions: ieee_next_up, ieee_int, ieee_max and friends

Fortran 2018 and 2023 completed the set. GNU Fortran 16.2 does not have ieee_next_up, ieee_next_down, ieee_int, ieee_real, ieee_max, ieee_max_mag, ieee_min and ieee_min_mag and has no round argument for ieee_rint; Flang 23 has them all, and the Flang standards-status page lists the changes for conformance with the new IEEE standard as implemented. (Whether a compiler has a name is easy to test: use, intrinsic :: ieee_arithmetic, only: name compiles or does not, and a check of that form for every procedure and type name of Tables 17.2 and 17.3 produced this list.) The program below uses all of them and needs Flang.

program newer_functions
  use, intrinsic :: iso_fortran_env, only: real32, real64, int32
  use, intrinsic :: ieee_arithmetic
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = real64
  real(dp) :: one, x, nan, pz, nz, a, b
  real(real32) :: y

  one = 1.0_dp + real(command_argument_count(), dp)
  x = 0.1_dp*one
  nan = ieee_value(one, ieee_quiet_nan)
  pz = 0.0_dp*one
  nz = -pz
  a = 1.5_dp*one
  b = -2.5_dp*one

  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'ieee_next_up(x)       = ', ieee_next_up(x)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'ieee_next_down(x)     = ', ieee_next_down(x)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'ieee_next_down(+0)    = ', ieee_next_down(pz)
  print '(a, es25.17e3)', 'ieee_next_up(-0)      = ', ieee_next_up(nz)
  print *
  print '(a)', 'F2023 maxima and minima of (1.5, -2.5), then (1.5, NaN), then (+0, -0):'
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'ieee_max', ieee_max(a, b), ieee_max(a, nan), ieee_max(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'ieee_max_mag', ieee_max_mag(a, b), ieee_max_mag(a, nan), ieee_max_mag(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'ieee_max_num', ieee_max_num(a, b), ieee_max_num(a, nan), ieee_max_num(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'ieee_max_num_mag', ieee_max_num_mag(a, b), ieee_max_num_mag(a, nan), ieee_max_num_mag(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'ieee_min', ieee_min(a, b), ieee_min(a, nan), ieee_min(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'ieee_min_mag', ieee_min_mag(a, b), ieee_min_mag(a, nan), ieee_min_mag(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'ieee_min_num', ieee_min_num(a, b), ieee_min_num(a, nan), ieee_min_num(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'ieee_min_num_mag', ieee_min_num_mag(a, b), ieee_min_num_mag(a, nan), ieee_min_num_mag(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'max (intrinsic)', max(a, b), max(a, nan), max(pz, nz)
  print *
  y = ieee_real(16777217_int32*int(one, int32), real32)   ! 2**24 + 1 is not representable in real32
  print '(a, f12.1)', 'ieee_real(2**24 + 1, real32)  = ', y
  print '(a, 2(1x, f5.1))', 'ieee_rint(2.5, up), (2.5, down): ', ieee_rint(2.5_dp*one, ieee_up), ieee_rint(2.5_dp*one, ieee_down)
  print '(a, 5(1x, i0))', 'ieee_int(2.5 up/down/to_zero/nearest), kind=int32: ', &
    ieee_int(2.5_dp*one, ieee_up, int32), ieee_int(2.5_dp*one, ieee_down, int32), &
    ieee_int(2.5_dp*one, ieee_to_zero, int32), ieee_int(2.5_dp*one, ieee_nearest, int32)
end program newer_functions

How the maxima and minima differ (17.11.17 to 17.11.24):

Function Result (X, Y)

ieee_max(x, y), ieee_min(x, y)

the larger or smaller value; a NaN in either argument gives a quiet NaN; of +0 and -0 the maximum is +0 and the minimum -0; F2023

ieee_max_mag(x, y), ieee_min_mag(x, y)

the argument of larger or smaller magnitude; if equal in magnitude, ieee_max or ieee_min; F2023

ieee_max_num(x, y), ieee_min_num(x, y)

as ieee_max and ieee_min, except that if exactly one argument is a quiet NaN the result is the other one; F2018

ieee_max_num_mag(x, y), ieee_min_num_mag(x, y)

the magnitude versions of the previous; F2018

For a signaling NaN, all eight raise invalid; F2023 changed the _num family so that a number paired with a signaling NaN gives the number (Fortran 2018 specified a NaN), and the standard lists this as a difference from Fortran 2018 whose interpretation can differ between the two editions (4.3.3). The next program, which runs on both compilers, shows the _num functions and the intrinsic max and min side by side on a NaN.

program max_num_gfortran
  use, intrinsic :: iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  use, intrinsic :: ieee_arithmetic
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = real64
  real(dp) :: one, nan, snan, pz, nz, a, b

  one = 1.0_dp + real(command_argument_count(), dp)
  nan = ieee_value(one, ieee_quiet_nan)
  snan = ieee_value(one, ieee_signaling_nan)
  pz = 0.0_dp*one
  nz = -pz
  a = 1.5_dp*one
  b = -2.5_dp*one

  print '(a, l1)', 'signaling NaN preserved by ieee_value: ', ieee_class(snan) == ieee_signaling_nan
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'ieee_max_num', ieee_max_num(a, b), ieee_max_num(a, nan), ieee_max_num(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'ieee_max_num_mag', ieee_max_num_mag(a, b), ieee_max_num_mag(a, nan), ieee_max_num_mag(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'ieee_min_num', ieee_min_num(a, b), ieee_min_num(a, nan), ieee_min_num(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'ieee_min_num_mag', ieee_min_num_mag(a, b), ieee_min_num_mag(a, nan), ieee_min_num_mag(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'max (intrinsic)', max(a, b), max(a, nan), max(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'min (intrinsic)', min(a, b), min(a, nan), min(pz, nz)
  print '(a22, 3(2x, g0))', 'max with NaN first', max(nan, a), max(nan, nan), max(nz, pz)
  print '(a, g0)', 'ieee_max_num(1.5, signaling NaN)   : ', ieee_max_num(a, snan)
end program max_num_gfortran

gfortran 16.2 (at -O0, the default of the strict build):

signaling NaN preserved by ieee_value: T
          ieee_max_num  1.5000000000000000  1.5000000000000000  0.0000000000000000
      ieee_max_num_mag  -2.5000000000000000  1.5000000000000000  0.0000000000000000
          ieee_min_num  -2.5000000000000000  1.5000000000000000  -0.0000000000000000
      ieee_min_num_mag  1.5000000000000000  1.5000000000000000  -0.0000000000000000
       max (intrinsic)  1.5000000000000000  1.5000000000000000  0.0000000000000000
       min (intrinsic)  -2.5000000000000000  1.5000000000000000  -0.0000000000000000
    max with NaN first  1.5000000000000000  NaN  0.0000000000000000
ieee_max_num(1.5, signaling NaN)   : NaN

Flang 23:

signaling NaN preserved by ieee_value: T
          ieee_max_num  1.5  1.5  0.
      ieee_max_num_mag  -2.5  1.5  0.
          ieee_min_num  -2.5  1.5  -0.
      ieee_min_num_mag  1.5  1.5  -0.
       max (intrinsic)  1.5  NaN  -0.
       min (intrinsic)  -2.5  NaN  -0.
    max with NaN first  1.5  NaN  0.
ieee_max_num(1.5, signaling NaN)   : 1.5

Source: J3/23-007r1: 4.3.3 Fortran 2018 compatibility, 17.11.19 IEEE_MAX_NUM and 16.9.135 MAX, GNU Fortran manual: MAX and MIN intrinsics with REAL NaN arguments

Two behaviours matter:

  • ieee_max_num(1.5, signaling NaN) is NaN under gfortran (the Fortran 2018 rule) and 1.5 under Flang (the Fortran 2023 rule).

  • The intrinsic max and min with a NaN are not defined by the standard, and the compilers do not agree: with a quiet NaN gfortran 16.2 at -O0 gives max(1.5, NaN) = 1.5 but max(NaN, NaN) = NaN, Flang gives NaN; and the answer can change with the optimization level (gfortran -O2 printed NaN for min(1.5, NaN), where -O0 printed 1.5). The GNU Fortran manual states that it deliberately does not specify the result and recommends testing the arguments with ieee_is_nan first. The same holds for maxval and minval; the Flang extensions page states that for these array reductions NaN elements are ignored unless all the unmasked elements are NaN (not tested here). Use the ieee_ versions when the behaviour must be defined, and wrap them in a small function when the program has to build with gfortran 16.2 and has to handle NaNs.

Worked examples

A reliable hypot

The length of a vector, sqrt(x**2 + y**2), overflows when x**2 is larger than huge although the result is representable, and underflows to zero when both squares are below tiny. The cure is to scale both arguments by a power of two before squaring, which is exact, and to undo the scaling afterwards. The module below implements it with exponent and scale, handles the infinities and NaNs as C99 hypot does (a NaN with an infinity gives infinity), and also implements the pattern of the standard’s example (17.12): try the fast way, check the flags, and fall back if an exception was signaled, while saving and restoring the caller’s status.

module heatflow_norms
  use, intrinsic :: iso_fortran_env, only: real64
  use, intrinsic :: ieee_arithmetic, only: ieee_get_flag, ieee_set_flag, ieee_overflow, ieee_underflow, &
                                            ieee_is_finite, ieee_is_nan, ieee_get_status, ieee_set_status, &
                                            ieee_status_type, ieee_all, ieee_value, ieee_positive_inf
  implicit none
  private
  public :: dp, naive_hypot, safe_hypot, checked_hypot
  integer, parameter :: dp = real64

contains

  !> sqrt(x*x + y*y): the squares can overflow or underflow although the result is representable.
  elemental function naive_hypot(x, y) result(h)
    real(dp), intent(in) :: x, y
    real(dp) :: h
    h = sqrt(x*x + y*y)
  end function naive_hypot

  !> Scale both arguments by a power of two so the squares stay in range, then undo the scaling.
  elemental function safe_hypot(x, y) result(h)
    real(dp), intent(in) :: x, y
    real(dp) :: h, ax, ay, big, small, ratio
    integer :: e
    ax = abs(x)
    ay = abs(y)
    if (.not. (ieee_is_finite(ax) .and. ieee_is_finite(ay))) then
      if (ieee_is_nan(ax) .and. .not. ieee_is_finite(ay) .and. .not. ieee_is_nan(ay)) then
        h = ay                                     ! hypot(NaN, Inf) = Inf, as in C99
      else if (ieee_is_nan(ay) .and. .not. ieee_is_finite(ax) .and. .not. ieee_is_nan(ax)) then
        h = ax
      else
        h = ax + ay                                ! Inf if either is infinite, NaN if either is a NaN
      end if
      return
    end if
    big = max(ax, ay)
    small = min(ax, ay)
    if (big <= 0.0_dp) then
      h = 0.0_dp
      return
    end if
    e = exponent(big)
    ratio = scale(small, -e)                       ! small / 2**e, exact unless it underflows
    h = scale(sqrt(scale(big, -e)**2 + ratio*ratio), e)
  end function safe_hypot

  !> The "try the fast way, check the flags, fall back" pattern of the standard's own example (17.12).
  function checked_hypot(x, y, fell_back) result(h)
    real(dp), intent(in) :: x, y
    logical, intent(out) :: fell_back
    real(dp) :: h
    type(ieee_status_type) :: status
    logical :: ovf, unf
    call ieee_get_status(status)                   ! save all flags and modes
    call ieee_set_flag(ieee_all, .false.)
    h = naive_hypot(x, y)
    call ieee_get_flag(ieee_overflow, ovf)
    call ieee_get_flag(ieee_underflow, unf)
    fell_back = ovf .or. unf
    call ieee_set_status(status)                   ! put the caller's flags back
    if (fell_back) h = safe_hypot(x, y)
  end function checked_hypot

end module heatflow_norms

program reliable_hypot
  use heatflow_norms
  use, intrinsic :: ieee_arithmetic, only: ieee_value, ieee_quiet_nan, ieee_positive_inf
  implicit none
  real(dp) :: xs(5), ys(5), scale_up, nan, inf
  logical :: fb
  integer :: i

  scale_up = 1.0_dp + real(command_argument_count(), dp)
  nan = ieee_value(scale_up, ieee_quiet_nan)
  inf = ieee_value(scale_up, ieee_positive_inf)
  xs = [3.0_dp, 3.0e200_dp, 3.0e-200_dp, 3.0e200_dp, 3.0_dp]*scale_up
  ys = [4.0_dp, 4.0e200_dp, 4.0e-200_dp, 1.0e-300_dp, 0.0_dp]*scale_up

  print '(a)', '           x            y        naive         safe    intrinsic       checked  fell back'
  do i = 1, 5
    print '(2(es12.3e3, 1x), 3(es12.4e3, 1x), es12.4e3, 5x, l1)', xs(i), ys(i), naive_hypot(xs(i), ys(i)), &
      safe_hypot(xs(i), ys(i)), hypot(xs(i), ys(i)), checked_hypot(xs(i), ys(i), fb), fb
  end do
  print '(a, 3(1x, g0))', 'special values: safe_hypot(Inf, NaN), (NaN, 1), (-Inf, 2): ', safe_hypot(inf, nan), &
    safe_hypot(nan, 1.0_dp), safe_hypot(-inf, 2.0_dp)
end program reliable_hypot

Output (identical with Flang 23):

           x            y        naive         safe    intrinsic       checked  fell back
  3.000E+000   4.000E+000  5.0000E+000  5.0000E+000  5.0000E+000  5.0000E+000     F
  3.000E+200   4.000E+200     Infinity  5.0000E+200  5.0000E+200  5.0000E+200     T
  3.000E-200   4.000E-200  0.0000E+000  5.0000E-200  5.0000E-200  5.0000E-200     T
  3.000E+200   1.000E-300     Infinity  3.0000E+200  3.0000E+200  3.0000E+200     T
  3.000E+000   0.000E+000  3.0000E+000  3.0000E+000  3.0000E+000  3.0000E+000     F
special values: safe_hypot(Inf, NaN), (NaN, 1), (-Inf, 2):  Inf NaN Inf

Source: J3/23-007r1: 17.12 Examples, 16.9.178 SCALE, 16.9.85 EXPONENT and 16.9.97 HYPOT, GNU Fortran manual: HYPOT

The naive version overflows to Infinity for 3e200 and 4e200 and underflows to 0 for 3e-200 and 4e-200; the scaled version and the intrinsic hypot (Fortran 2008) agree. The checked_hypot row shows T in the last column exactly when the naive way raised overflow or underflow. The intrinsic hypot is the better choice in production; the point is the technique. A related technique, compensated summation, is in the compiler-options section below.

Worked example: detecting a diverging heatflow run

The explicit FTCS scheme of the heatflow solver is stable only if alpha * dt / dx**2 is at most 0.25 in two dimensions. Beyond that, rounding errors grow by a factor at each step, and after a few thousand steps the values overflow and then turn to NaN. The program uses the kernel ftcs_sweep of the module heatflow_kernels (the explicit step used by the solvers, see Object Oriented Programming) and checks the residual of each step with ieee_is_finite instead of waiting for garbage output. It was built together with the two module files: gfortran ... heatflow_kinds.f90 heatflow_kernels.f90 13_divergence_guard.f90.

! Detect a diverging explicit (FTCS) heat-flow run with IEEE tests instead of waiting for garbage output.
program divergence_guard
  use heatflow_kinds, only: dp, ip
  use heatflow_kernels, only: ftcs_sweep
  use, intrinsic :: ieee_arithmetic, only: ieee_is_finite, ieee_get_flag, ieee_set_flag, ieee_all, &
                                            ieee_overflow, ieee_invalid, ieee_flag_type
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: n = 21
  real(dp), parameter :: dx = 1.0_dp/(n - 1), alpha = 1.0_dp
  real(dp) :: dt_stable, dt_unstable

  dt_stable = 0.2_dp*dx**2/alpha          ! alpha*dt/dx**2 = 0.2, below the 2D limit of 0.25
  dt_unstable = 0.3_dp*dx**2/alpha        ! 0.3 is above the limit
  call run('stable  ', dt_stable)
  call run('unstable', dt_unstable)

contains

  subroutine run(label, dt)
    character(len=*), intent(in) :: label
    real(dp), intent(in) :: dt
    real(dp) :: u(n, n), unew(n, n), residual
    integer(ip) :: step
    logical :: overflowed, invalid

    u = 0.0_dp
    u((n + 1)/2, (n + 1)/2) = 100.0_dp
    unew = u
    call ieee_set_flag(ieee_all, .false.)
    do step = 1, 4000
      call ftcs_sweep(u, unew, alpha, dt, dx, dx, residual)
      u = unew
      if (.not. ieee_is_finite(residual)) then
        call ieee_get_flag(ieee_overflow, overflowed)
        call ieee_get_flag(ieee_invalid, invalid)
        print '(a, a, i0, a, l1, a, l1)', label, ': residual is not finite at step ', step, &
          '; overflow flag ', overflowed, ', invalid flag ', invalid
        return
      end if
    end do
    print '(a, a, es10.3e3, a, f7.3)', label, ': finished, last residual ', residual, ', max temperature ', maxval(u)
  end subroutine run

end program divergence_guard

Output (identical with Flang 23):

stable  : finished, last residual 6.351E-020, max temperature   0.000
unstable: residual is not finite at step 2155; overflow flag T, invalid flag F

Source: J3/23-007r1: 17.11.12 IEEE_IS_FINITE and 17.3 The exceptions

The stable run, at a ratio of 0.2, ends with a residual of 6.4E-20 and the unstable one, at 0.3, makes the residual non-finite at step 2155 with the overflow flag signaling. Detecting the blow-up in the first step it becomes non-finite is cheap: one ieee_is_finite per step on a scalar that the loop already computes. The flags are a second channel: the ieee_overflow flag was raised by the kernel, a procedure called from here, and stays signaling in the caller on return (17.3). In a larger program, leave halting off, check ieee_is_finite on summary quantities, and report which flags are signaling when you stop.

Compiler options that change floating-point semantics

The standard allows the compiler to evaluate any mathematically equivalent expression (10.1.5.2.4). Optimization options go far beyond that, and they interact with every guarantee above: the NaN tests, the flags, the rounding modes and the order of a sum. The table lists what the options do according to the vendors' documentation.

Option Effect Source

-ffast-math (gfortran, GCC)

sets -fno-math-errno, -funsafe-math-optimizations, -ffinite-math-only, -fno-rounding-math, -fno-signaling-nans, -fcx-limited-range and -fexcess-precision=fast; no -O level enables it except -Ofast

GCC manual: Optimize Options

-Ofast (gfortran)

all of -O3, plus -ffast-math, -fallow-store-data-races, -fstack-arrays and -fno-protect-parens

GCC manual: Optimize Options

-ffinite-math-only

assume arguments and results are not NaN or infinity, so ieee_is_nan and x /= x may become false

GCC manual

-fno-signed-zeros

ignore the sign of zero, so x + 0.0 and 0.0 * x can be simplified

GCC manual

-fno-trapping-math

assume floating-point operations cannot generate user-visible traps; it requires -fno-signaling-nans to be in effect

GCC manual

-funsafe-math-optimizations

enables -fno-signed-zeros, -fno-trapping-math, -fassociative-math and -freciprocal-math; when used at link time may include startup files that change the FPU control word

GCC manual

-fassociative-math

reassociate sums, which changes results; for Fortran it is enabled automatically when both -fno-signed-zeros and -fno-trapping-math are in effect

GCC manual

-fno-protect-parens

lets the compiler reorder real and complex expressions across parentheses; parentheses are honored by default, except under -Ofast; reassociation also needs -fno-signed-zeros and -fno-trapping-math

GNU Fortran manual: code generation options

-frounding-math, -fsignaling-nans

the options the manual recommends for the IEEE modules; the first disables constant folding of floating-point expressions and unsafe transformations, the second assumes signaling NaNs can trap

GCC manual; GNU Fortran manual: IEEE modules

-ffp-contract=off|fast

forming of fused multiply-add where the target has it; the GCC manual gives fast as the default except for C in a strict standard mode, and the results below confirm contraction at -O2 in gfortran

GCC manual

-ffpe-trap=list

enable traps on invalid, zero, overflow, underflow, inexact, denormal; a trap cannot be disabled again except by clearing the whole list with none

GNU Fortran manual: debugging options

-ffpe-summary=list

which flags to list at stop and error stop

GNU Fortran manual: debugging options

-ffast-math (Flang)

-fno-honor-infinities -fno-honor-nans -fassociative-math -freciprocal-math -fapprox-func -fno-signed-zeros -ffp-contract=fast, plus -fcomplex-arithmetic=basic; links crtfastmath.o, which sets the flush-to-zero bits for the whole program on processors where it applies

Flang documentation: Flang Driver

-ffp-contract=, -fno-signed-zeros (Flang)

as above, selectable separately

Flang --help

-fp-model=precise|fast[=1|2]|consistent|strict|source (Intel ifx)

value-safe, more aggressive, reproducible across microarchitectures (disables FMA contraction), strict (allows changing the floating-point environment) or source-rounded; the default is -fp-model=fast, and fast=2 does not recognise NaN or infinities

Intel Fortran Compiler: fp-model, fp

The Flang documentation also says that the GCC and gfortran definition of -ffast-math is wider, because it also includes -fno-trapping-math, -fno-rounding-math and -fsignaling-nans; Flang does not list them because it has no support for strict floating point yet and always behaves as if they were in effect.

What -ffast-math does to a program

The next program has the two kinds of damage in one place. plain_sum adds ten million real32 values of 0.1 in a loop, kahan_sum does it with compensated (Kahan) summation (it keeps the rounding error of each addition in a second variable and feeds it back), and the last two lines test a NaN in two ways.

module kahan
  use, intrinsic :: iso_fortran_env, only: real32
  implicit none
  private
  public :: plain_sum, kahan_sum
  integer, parameter :: sp = real32
contains

  function plain_sum(x) result(s)
    real(sp), intent(in) :: x(:)
    real(sp) :: s
    integer :: i
    s = 0.0_sp
    do i = 1, size(x)
      s = s + x(i)
    end do
  end function plain_sum

  ! Compensated (Kahan) summation: c carries the low-order bits lost by each addition.
  function kahan_sum(x) result(s)
    real(sp), intent(in) :: x(:)
    real(sp) :: s, c, y, t
    integer :: i
    s = 0.0_sp
    c = 0.0_sp
    do i = 1, size(x)
      y = x(i) - c
      t = s + y
      c = (t - s) - y        ! algebraically zero; exactly the rounding error of the addition
      s = t
    end do
  end function kahan_sum

end module kahan

program fast_math
  use, intrinsic :: iso_fortran_env, only: real32, real64
  use, intrinsic :: ieee_arithmetic, only: ieee_is_nan, ieee_value, ieee_quiet_nan, ieee_quiet_eq
  use kahan, only: plain_sum, kahan_sum
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: sp = real32
  real(sp), allocatable :: x(:)
  real(sp) :: nan, y
  integer :: n

  n = 10000000 + command_argument_count()
  allocate (x(n), source=0.1_sp)

  print '(a, f14.2)', 'exact sum 10^7 * 0.1 (in real32 data) : ', real(n, real64)*real(0.1_sp, real64)
  print '(a, f14.2)', 'plain_sum                             : ', plain_sum(x)
  print '(a, f14.2)', 'kahan_sum                             : ', kahan_sum(x)

  nan = ieee_value(nan, ieee_quiet_nan)
  y = nan*real(n, sp)
  print '(a, l1)', 'ieee_is_nan(y) (should be T)          : ', ieee_is_nan(y)
  print '(a, l1)', '.not. ieee_quiet_eq(y, y) (should be T): ', .not. ieee_quiet_eq(y, y)
end program fast_math

At the default -O0 and at -O2 and -O3 (no fast-math), with both compilers:

plain_sum                             :     1087937.00
kahan_sum                             :     1000000.00
ieee_is_nan(y) (should be T)          : T
.not. ieee_quiet_eq(y, y) (should be T): T

Source: GCC manual: Options that control optimization, Flang documentation: Flang Driver

What the table says:

  • The exact sum is 1000000.01. The naive loop returns 1087937: ten million additions of a small number to a growing total, each rounded, drift by almost 9%. Compensated summation gives 1000000.00, the correctly rounded value. (Summing in real64, or using the intrinsic sum on real64 data, would also be accurate.)

  • -ffast-math removes the compensation. With -fassociative-math (enabled by -ffast-math) the compiler is allowed to regard (t - s) - y as zero, and the compensated sum collapses to the naive one. Adding -fno-associative-math brings the Kahan sum back. A numerically careful routine can be silently ruined by a build option.

  • -Ofast vectorizes the reduction (adds in a different order) and gives a third answer, 975599.12, which is not better or worse in principle, only different. The sum of a large array depends on the compiler, the option and the processor vector width, so exact reproducibility of sums needs a fixed order or compensation.

  • The NaN tests are removed under -ffast-math in both compilers: ieee_is_nan(y) and the quiet comparison of y with itself print F for a value that really is a NaN. Under -ffinite-math-only the compiler is told that NaNs cannot occur, so it believes the answer. Any code that checks NaN must not be built with fast-math: put it in a separate source file with its own options, or do not use fast-math for the project.

Fused multiply-add and expression contraction

A processor with a fused multiply-add instruction can compute a*b + c in one step with one rounding. The compiler is allowed to use it for an expression written as a multiplication followed by an addition, because it is a mathematically equivalent expression (10.1.5.2.4), and parentheses do not stop it: the standard’s rule is about the integrity of the parenthesized operation, not about the rounding of its intermediate value. Results change at the last bit, between optimization levels of the same compiler.

program contraction
  use, intrinsic :: iso_fortran_env, only: real32, real64
  implicit none
  real(real32) :: a, c, r
  a = (1.0_real32 + 2.0_real32**(-12))*real(1 + command_argument_count(), real32)
  c = -1.0_real32
  r = a*a + c
  print '(a, es24.16e3)', 'a*a + c, as written       : ', real(r, real64)
  print '(a, es24.16e3)', 'exact value of a*a + c    : ', real(a, real64)*real(a, real64) + real(c, real64)
end program contraction

Built with gfortran 16.2 and with Flang 23 (the strict -O0 build of the page prints the first line):

Build a*a + c as written (exact value 4.8834085E-04)

gfortran -O0 and Flang -O0

4.8828125E-04 (two roundings)

gfortran -O2 and Flang -O2

4.8834085E-04 (one rounding, a fused multiply-add)

gfortran -O2 -ffp-contract=off and Flang -O2 -ffp-contract=off

4.8828125E-04

gfortran -O3 -ffast-math, -Ofast and Flang -O2 -ffast-math

4.8834085E-04

Source: J3/23-007r1: 10.1.5.2.4 Evaluation of numeric intrinsic operations, GCC manual: -ffp-contract

Both compilers contract at -O2 on this processor with the default options, and both stop when given -ffp-contract=off. The processor matters: this container is an aarch64 one, where a fused multiply-add is part of the base instruction set; on x86-64 builds without -march flags that enable FMA, the same program prints the two-rounding result at all optimization levels (not checked here). The rule for reproducible results across machines and compilers is to use ieee_fma where a single rounding is wanted and -ffp-contract=off where it is not, and to keep the -O level out of the correctness argument. Intel ifx’s -fp-model=consistent also disables the contraction, as its manual states.

Fortran IEEE facilities next to C’s fenv.h

The C language has the same facilities in <fenv.h> and <math.h>, described in Numbers and Math. The correspondence is close enough to move knowledge in both directions and to write code at the boundary of a bind(c) interface (see Interoperability with C).

The floating-point status is per thread in C and per image in Fortran. A Fortran procedure that is called from C and signals an exception leaves the flags signaling in the caller (17.3), which is what the C side usually wants. If the Fortran code sets a rounding mode, it must restore it before returning (17.4).

Where the books are outdated

The two Fortran books consulted for this section were used for the concepts they cover (the IEEE concepts, the three modules, flags, halting, rounding and underflow modes, the ieee_support_* inquiries and the worked examples). Material written before Fortran 2018 and 2023, which includes parts of both, differs from the current standard and from current practice in the following ways:

Area Outdated material, current approach

IEEE references

the chapter on IEEE arithmetic in the older of the two books cites IEEE 754-2008 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 60559:2011; the current documents are IEEE 754-2019 and ISO/IEC 60559:2020, which Fortran 2023 adopts, and clause 17 of Fortran 2023 is written against them

ieee_max_num family and new functions

written before Fortran 2023, where ieee_max, ieee_min and the _mag variants are new and a number paired with a signaling NaN gives the number in the _num functions

Pure and simple

written before Fortran 2023 made the rounding, underflow, modes and status procedures pure and simple (the compilers tested still treat the setters as impure)

Compiler support

no statement of which compiler implements which function; GNU Fortran 16.2 lacks ieee_next_up, ieee_next_down, ieee_int, ieee_real, ieee_max, ieee_min, the _mag variants and the round argument of ieee_rint, while LLVM Flang 23 has them all, and the two differ on flags on entry to a procedure, on the signaling of <, on hexadecimal input and EX output and on underflow control

Optimization and exceptions

older teaching material rarely warns that an unused computation may never signal, that -ffast-math removes NaN tests and compensated sums, or that the compiler fuses a multiplication and an addition by default at -O2; this page demonstrates each

real*8, real*16 and double precision

the older ways to name the kinds; use real64, real128 and selected_real_kind or ieee_selected_real_kind, as in the other pages of this section

Pitfalls

  • Comparing reals with == works by luck in one kind and fails in another. Compare with a tolerance, count ulps, or use ieee_quiet_eq when exactness is the intent.

  • Testing for NaN with x /= x is folded by -ffast-math. Use ieee_is_nan, and keep NaN-aware code out of fast-math builds.

  • A tolerance copied from another kind: 1.0e-6 is a few ulps in real32 and a million ulps in real64. Derive it from epsilon(x).

  • Using epsilon as the smallest positive number: that is tiny (normal) or the smallest subnormal. epsilon is the spacing at 1.

  • Flags tested in a helper procedure that the compiler may reset on entry (Flang does, gfortran does not). Read flags in the procedure that computes.

  • Computations whose result is not used do not signal on an optimizing compiler.

  • Formatted output can leave a flag signaling (g0 did under gfortran 16.2) and, under gfortran, follows the current rounding mode. Read the flags before printing, and restore the mode before printing.

  • Changing the rounding mode and then calling a library that assumes round-to-nearest. Restore it, ideally with ieee_get_modes and ieee_set_modes around the region.

  • Calling an IEEE function without checking the support inquiry, especially ieee_support_underflow_control before ieee_set_underflow_mode, which the standard forbids when it is false.

  • Assuming every compiler has the F2018 and F2023 functions: ieee_next_up, ieee_int, ieee_max and others are missing in gfortran 16.2.

  • Using the intrinsic max or min on data that may contain a NaN: the result is not defined and depends on the compiler and the optimization level.

  • Trapping on underflow or inexact: they happen in almost every program, so -ffpe-trap=invalid,zero,overflow is the sensible set; the traps are a hardware feature that some Arm processors do not have.

  • Reading the sign of zero: x < 0.0 is false for -0.0; use ieee_signbit or ieee_is_negative.

  • Trusting a sum: a loop over millions of values, a reduction vectorized by the compiler and a parallel reduction give different results. Compare with a tolerance and, where accuracy matters, use compensated summation (and no -ffast-math).

  • Fast-math on shared libraries: with -ffast-math the linker may add startup code that sets the flush-to-zero bits for the whole program, including libraries compiled without it.

See also Best Practices and Style, Common Gotchas and Pitfalls and Performance and Memory Layout.
